relationships.reason: The two-pointer technique is an algorithmic pattern that operates directly on arrays by manipulating index variables to traverse the elements.
The sliding window technique is an array-based approach that expands and contracts a contiguous subrange of an array using indexing.
Understanding how arrays are indexed is explicitly noted as a prerequisite to understanding how a hash table's internal buckets function.
Trees generalize the node-and-pointer architecture of linked lists (branching to multiple children instead of pointing to one 'next' node), making linked lists a conceptual stepping stone.
A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a specialized type of tree; understanding tree terminology (nodes, root, children, height) is strictly necessary to comprehend BST properties.
Binary search is an algorithm specifically designed to find elements within a sorted array, requiring direct familiarity with array structures and index lookups.
Tree traversal algorithms (BFS and DFS) cannot be understood without a foundational understanding of tree structures and hierarchical node structures.
The text explicitly states that understanding queues and stacks is a prerequisite because BFS is implemented using a queue and DFS is implemented using a stack.
A heap is a specialized tree-based structure, and the text notes that understanding basic tree structure and terminology is necessary before heaps make sense.
